steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our dataset distillation paper. It should explain why existing distillation methods stop working as the synthetic set gets larger, connect this to easy vs. hard patterns in trajectory matching, and present our difficulty-aligned approach that makes distillation lossless.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Dataset distillation: goal, method families, success with tiny synthetic sets, applications
- Problem: gap to full data; methods degrade as IPC grows
- Observation: TM methods learn easy vs. hard patterns depending on trajectory stage
- Effect of easy/hard patterns depends on IPC
- Our method: align pattern difficulty with dataset size; results (lossless)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Dataset distillation (DD)
  - distill large dataset into small synthetic one; models trained on it perform like on original
  - algorithms: gradient matching (cite), kernel inducing points (cite), distribution matching (cite), trajectory matching (cite)
  - great success with extremely small synthetic sets; MTT (cite): 71.6% test acc on CIFAR-10 with 1% of data
  - applications: continual learning (cite), privacy protection (cite), neural architecture search (cite)
- Problem
  - success with very few IPC (images-per-class), but big gap to full real data
  - intuitive fix: bigger synthetic set; but as IPC grows, methods less effective, even worse than random selection (cite)
  - this paper: why they become ineffective; first to circumvent -> lossless dataset distillation
- Observation on learned patterns (TM-based methods as example (cite))
  - distillation = embedding informative patterns into synthetic samples
  - TM: match training trajectories of surrogate models on synthetic vs. real data
  - DNNs learn easy patterns early, hard patterns later (cite)
  - so data properties depend on teacher training stage sampled (early/late): early -> easy, late -> hard patterns
- Easy vs. hard depending on IPC
  - low IPC: easy patterns best, explain larger part of real distribution than same number of hard samples
  - large synthetic set: hard samples optimal, union covers easy + “long-tail” hard samples
  - easy patterns at high IPC worse than random selection: images collapse to mean patterns, miss long tail
  - previous methods default to easy patterns -> ineffective at high IPC
- Our method
  - align difficulty of learned patterns with size of distilled dataset, effective at low and high IPC
  - control difficulty by matching only trajectories of a specified training phase
  - learn easy then hard patterns sequentially -> stable enough to learn soft labels; further improvement
  - state of the art at low and high IPC
  - CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 to 1/5, Tiny ImageNet to 1/10 without performance loss on ConvNet; first lossless method

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Dataset distillation (DD) tries to distill a large dataset into a small synthetic one, so that models that are trained on the distilled dataset have similar performance as models trained on the original dataset. In recent years several algorithms were proposed for this important topic, for example gradient matching, kernel inducing points, distribution matching, and trajectory matching. Until now dataset distillation has been very successful when the synthetic sets are extremely small. For example MTT gets 71.6% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 with only 1% of the original data size. Because of this impressive performance it was applied to a variety of downstream tasks like continual learning, privacy protection, and neural architecture search.

But even though previous DD methods were very successful with very few IPC (images-per-class), there is still a big gap between the performance of their distilled datasets and the full real datasets. To reduce this gap, the intuitive idea is to make the synthetic dataset bigger. Unfortunately, when IPC increases, previous distillation methods mysteriously become less effective and even perform worse than random selection. In this paper we give an answer to why previous dataset distillation methods become ineffective when IPC increases, and doing so we are the first to get around this issue, which lets us achieve lossless dataset distillation.

- Observation on learned patterns (TM-based methods as example)
  - DD = embedding informative patterns into synthetic samples; TM matches training trajectories of surrogate models on synthetic vs. real data
  - DNNs learn easy patterns early, hard later -> early trajectories give easy, late give hard patterns
- Easy vs. hard depending on IPC
  - low IPC: easy patterns best; large set: hard samples optimal, union covers easy + “long-tail” hard
  - easy patterns at high IPC worse than random selection (collapse to mean patterns); previous methods default to easy
- Our method
  - align difficulty with dataset size; match only trajectories of a specified training phase
  - learn easy then hard sequentially -> soft labels; state of the art
  - CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 to 1/5, Tiny ImageNet to 1/10, no loss on ConvNet; first lossless

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Dataset distillation (DD) tries to distill a large dataset into a small synthetic one, so that models that are trained on the distilled dataset have similar performance as models trained on the original dataset. In recent years several algorithms were proposed for this important topic, for example gradient matching, kernel inducing points, distribution matching, and trajectory matching. Until now dataset distillation has been very successful when the synthetic sets are extremely small. For example MTT gets 71.6% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 with only 1% of the original data size. Because of this impressive performance it was applied to a variety of downstream tasks like continual learning, privacy protection, and neural architecture search.

But even though previous DD methods were very successful with very few IPC (images-per-class), there is still a big gap between the performance of their distilled datasets and the full real datasets. To reduce this gap, the intuitive idea is to make the synthetic dataset bigger. Unfortunately, when IPC increases, previous distillation methods mysteriously become less effective and even perform worse than random selection. In this paper we give an answer to why previous dataset distillation methods become ineffective when IPC increases, and doing so we are the first to get around this issue, which lets us achieve lossless dataset distillation.

We start by looking at the patterns the synthetic data learns, and we take trajectory matching (TM) based distillation methods as an example. In general, dataset distillation can be seen as embedding informative patterns into a set of synthetic samples. In TM-based methods the synthetic data learns patterns by matching the training trajectories of surrogate models that are optimized on the synthetic dataset and on the real one. Prior work found that deep neural networks (DNNs) usually learn to recognize easy patterns early in training and hard patterns later. So we note that the properties of the data generated by TM-based methods are very different depending on which teacher training stage we sample our trajectories from (early or late). Matching early trajectories makes the synthetic data learn easy patterns, and matching late trajectories makes it learn hard patterns.

Then we show empirically that the effect of learning easy and hard patterns changes with the size of the synthetic dataset (i.e., IPC). When IPC is low, easy patterns are the most beneficial, since they explain a larger part of the real data distribution than the same number of hard samples. But when the synthetic set is large enough, learning hard samples becomes optimal, since their union covers both the easy and the “long-tail” hard samples of the real data. Actually, learning easy patterns at high IPC is worse than random selection, because the synthetic images collapse towards the mean patterns of the distribution and do not capture the long-tail parts anymore. Previous distillation methods by default distill easy patterns, and this is why they are ineffective at high IPC.

These findings motivate us to align the difficulty of the learned patterns with the size of the distilled dataset, so that our method stays effective at both low and high IPC. Our experiments show that for TM-based methods we can control how difficult the generated patterns are by only matching the trajectories of a specified training phase. This way our method works well at both low and high IPC. We also propose to learn easy and hard patterns one after another, which makes the optimization stable enough to learn soft labels during distillation, and this brings another significant improvement. Our method gets state-of-the-art performance at both low and high IPC. In particular, we distill CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 to 1/5 and Tiny ImageNet to 1/10 of their original sizes without any loss of performance on ConvNet, which is the first lossless method of dataset distillation.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Dataset distillation (DD) aims at distilling a large dataset into a small synthetic one, such that models trained on the distilled dataset have similar performance to those trained on the original dataset. In recent years, several algorithms have been proposed for this important topic, such as gradient matching [1,2,3,4], kernel inducing points [5,6], distribution matching [7,8,9], and trajectory matching [10,11,12]. So far, dataset distillation has been very successful in the regime of extremely small synthetic sets. For example, MTT [10] achieves 71.6% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 using only 1% of the original data size. This impressive performance has led to its application in a variety of downstream tasks such as continual learning [13,14], privacy protection [15,16,17,18,19], and neural architecture search [20,21].

However, although previous DD methods have achieved great success with very few IPC (images-per-class), a significant gap remains between the performance of their distilled datasets and the full, real counterparts. To minimize this gap, one would intuitively increase the size of the synthetic dataset. Unfortunately, as IPC increases, previous distillation methods mysteriously become less effective, even performing worse than random selection [22,23]. In this paper, we offer an answer as to why previous dataset distillation methods become ineffective as IPC increases and, in doing so, are the first to circumvent this issue, which allows us to achieve lossless dataset distillation.

We start by observing the patterns learned by the synthetic data, taking trajectory matching (TM) based distillation methods [10,12] as an example. Generally, dataset distillation can be viewed as embedding informative patterns into a set of synthetic samples. For TM-based methods, the synthetic data learns patterns by matching the training trajectories of surrogate models optimized over the synthetic dataset and the real one. According to [24], deep neural networks (DNNs) typically learn to recognize easy patterns early in training and hard patterns later on. As a result, the properties of the data generated by TM-based methods vary widely depending on which teacher training stage (early or late) we sample our trajectories from. Specifically, matching early or late trajectories causes the synthetic data to learn easy or hard patterns, respectively.

We then empirically show that the effect of learning easy and hard patterns varies with the size of the synthetic dataset (i.e., IPC). In low-IPC settings, easy patterns are the most beneficial, since they explain a larger portion of the real data distribution than an equivalent number of hard samples. However, with a sufficiently large synthetic set, learning hard samples becomes optimal, since their union covers both the easy and the “long-tail” hard samples of the real data. In fact, learning easy patterns in the high-IPC setting performs worse than random selection, because the synthetic images collapse towards the mean patterns of the distribution and can no longer capture the long-tail parts. Previous distillation methods default to distilling easy patterns, which leads to their ineffectiveness in high-IPC cases.

These findings motivate us to align the difficulty of the learned patterns with the size of the distilled dataset, in order to keep our method effective in both low and high IPC cases. Our experiments show that, for TM-based methods, we can control the difficulty of the generated patterns by matching only the trajectories of a specified training phase. In this way, our method works well in both low and high IPC settings. Furthermore, we propose to learn easy and hard patterns sequentially, which makes the optimization stable enough to learn soft labels during distillation and brings further significant improvement. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both low and high IPC cases. Notably, we distill CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 to 1/5 and Tiny ImageNet to 1/10 of their original sizes without any performance loss on ConvNet, offering the first lossless method of dataset distillation.
